scenes.headline: Structured Logging
scenes.subtitle: Observability for production pipelines
scenes.narration: When a job fails at three in the morning, its logs are often all you have to work with, and structured logging is what makes those logs searchable, filterable, and genuinely useful.

scenes.headline: print vs logging
scenes.narration: A print statement always dumps to stdout with no severity, no timestamp, and no way to turn it off. The logging module gives you severity levels you can filter, handlers that route messages to files or external systems, formatters that add timestamps and context, and support for structured fields. For anything running in production, logging is the clear choice over print.

scenes.headline: Log levels
scenes.narration: DEBUG carries fine-grained detail useful while developing but too noisy for production. INFO records normal, expected progress through a run. WARNING flags something unexpected that the job handled and recovered from. ERROR and CRITICAL mark genuine failures. Because you set a threshold level, you can run verbose in development and quiet in production without editing a single line of code.

scenes.headline: Configuring a logger
scenes.code:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format='%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s',
)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
logger.info('loaded %d rows', len(rows))
scenes.narration: The basicConfig call sets the minimum level and a format that stamps each line with a timestamp, level, and logger name. Fetching a logger with __name__ gives each module its own named logger, which makes filtering by source easy later. Passing the row count as an argument rather than formatting it into the string uses lazy interpolation, so the message is only built if it's actually emitted.

scenes.headline: Structured context
scenes.narration: Passing an extra dictionary attaches structured fields like the user id and pipeline stage to a log record. With a JSON formatter, those fields become first-class, queryable attributes in your log platform rather than text buried in a message. That lets you filter and aggregate across millions of lines, for instance every event for one user, or every failure in the transform stage.

scenes.text: Use the logging module with named loggers and levels, never print, and log structured context for search.
scenes.narration: Named loggers, sensible levels, and structured context fields together turn scattered log lines into real observability you can actually query.
